opus-5.5.text:
I think brute-force scaling has been one of the most important lessons of the past decade, and honestly, I was a bit skeptical of it early in my career. Coming from robotics and computer graphics, I was trained to think that the right way to solve a problem was to understand its structure deeply: write down the physics, design a clever controller, hand-engineer the right representation. And for a long time that worked reasonably well for narrow tasks.

But what we've seen with large language models, and increasingly in vision, is that when you scale compute and data together, you get capabilities that nobody explicitly designed. Rich Sutton's "bitter lesson" captures this well: general methods that leverage computation tend to win in the long run over methods that rely on human-crafted knowledge. I've come to believe that's largely true.

That said, I think robotics is a special case worth talking about. In language, the internet gave us an enormous pre-existing dataset almost for free. In robotics, we don't have that. Every piece of robot data has to be collected physically, through teleoperation, autonomous trials, or simulation, and that's expensive and slow. So in our field, "brute force" isn't just about buying more GPUs. It's about figuring out how to scale the data engine itself. That's why I spend a lot of time thinking about simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and how to leverage internet-scale vision and language models as a prior so that robots don't have to learn everything from scratch.

So my view is that scaling is necessary but not sufficient. It's the engine, but you still need to make smart choices about what to scale, how to get the data, and what architecture can absorb it effectively. The breakthroughs come when a scalable method meets a scalable data source. In language we found that combination first. In robotics, I think we're just now starting to find it, and that's what makes this moment so exciting.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling compute and data together is necessary and calls scaling “the engine” behind breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says scaling is “necessary but not sufficient” and adds that choices about data and architecture also matter.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say brute-force scaling has been the single most reliable driver of progress over the past decade, and I think people who are uncomfortable with that fact tend to underestimate it. The bitter lesson is real: methods that leverage computation keep beating methods that leverage human cleverness about the problem structure. We saw it with vision, with language, and we're seeing it now in robotics with large-scale data collection and simulation.

But I want to be careful about the word "brute-force," because it hides a lot of craft. Scaling only works if you've found the right thing to scale. For language, the recipe was next-token prediction on internet text, and once that was found, the path was mostly about engineering and capital. In robotics, we're still searching for that recipe. You can't just download a trillion tokens of robot experience from the web. So a huge amount of the work is figuring out what data actually transfers, how simulation and real-world experience can be combined, and what the right objective is. Those are research questions, not compute questions.

So my view is that scaling is necessary but not sufficient. It's the amplifier. If the underlying idea is right, scaling turns it into a breakthrough. If the idea is wrong, scaling just gives you a very expensive failure. The interesting work right now, at least in embodied AI, is identifying which ideas deserve the compute, and building the data engines that make scaling possible at all.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says scaling is necessary and discusses scaling compute and data as a driver of AI progress.

r002.rationale: The candidate explicitly says scaling is “not sufficient” and explains that scaling a wrong idea can produce an expensive failure.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling compute and data is a very powerful approach, but I wouldn’t call it the whole recipe for breakthroughs. You can have an idea that doesn’t work at a small scale, and then, with enough computation and enough data, it suddenly becomes useful. So we should take scaling seriously rather than dismiss it as just brute force.

At the same time, what you scale matters. Is the data relevant? Is the learning objective actually aligned with the capability you want? Can you evaluate whether the system is improving? More compute doesn’t automatically solve those problems.

I see scaling and research as complementary. Better algorithms make compute more productive, and larger-scale experiments reveal limitations that inspire new algorithms. The interesting question is where scaling continues to deliver progress and where we need a different idea.

r001.rationale: The response calls scaling powerful and says it can make some ideas useful, but does not present scaling compute and data as necessary for AI breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response says scaling is not the whole recipe and that more compute does not automatically solve data, objective, or evaluation problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling compute and data is a powerful tool, but it’s not the whole story. Calling it “brute force” can obscure how much research goes into making that scale useful—choosing the right architecture, training objective, and data.

In robotics, for example, collecting more data is valuable, but what the robot experiences matters enormously. Repeating the same behavior in the same environment may add less than a smaller amount of diverse experience that exposes meaningful failures.

So I wouldn’t frame it as scaling versus innovation. Better methods make scaling more effective, and scaling lets us discover limitations that motivate better methods. The important question is: what is the bottleneck, and will more compute or data actually address it?

r001.rationale: The response calls scaling compute and data a powerful tool, but does not say it is necessary for AI breakthroughs.

r002.rationale: The response says scaling is “not the whole story” and explains that better methods are also needed.
